<METHOD_NAME>Set-Theoretic Prohibition Condition</METHOD_NAME>
<METHOD_DESCRIPTION>Replaces the verbal description of a 3-clique with a formal set-theoretic condition (the remaining two materials in S are both members of R_x). This prevents models from pattern-matching phrase structures like "a primary pair... alongside a third material" to standard triangle-finding templates, forcing them to reason about the sets directly.</METHOD_DESCRIPTION>
<METHOD_NOVEL>yes</METHOD_NOVEL>

<STATEMENT>
# Problem C — Cargo Prohibition Protocol

Time limit: 2 s   Memory limit: 256 MB

A logistics firm operates a shipping route for hazardous materials. Certain pairs of these materials are highly reactive and are strictly prohibited from sharing a vessel.

The proposed loading schedule is structurally impossible to fulfill. You must produce a definitive proof of this impossibility to trigger an automatic schedule rejection.

To establish this proof, you are required to isolate a "deadlock" configuration. Let $R_k$ denote the set of materials that are explicitly prohibited from sharing a vessel with material $k$. A deadlock configuration is defined as a set $S$ of exactly three distinct materials where, for any chosen material $x \in S$, the remaining two materials in $S$ are both members of $R_x$.

Because the automated auditing system requires deterministic reporting, it will not accept an arbitrary deadlock configuration. The system demands the canonical proof, meaning you must systematically ensure no earlier configuration could have been reported.

## Input
The first line provides two integers $n$ and $m$ ($3 \le n \le 2000$, $3 \le m \le \min(n(n-1)/2, 2 \cdot 10^5)$), indicating the number of hazardous materials and the number of prohibited pairs. The materials are identified by integers from $1$ to $n$.
Each of the following $m$ lines contains two integers $u$ and $v$ ($1 \le u, v \le n$, $u \ne v$) — a pair of materials that are prohibited from sharing a vessel. 
It is guaranteed that the input contains at least one deadlock configuration of three materials.

## Output
Output a single line containing three integers $a$, $b$, and $c$ ($a < b < c$), representing the identifiers of the materials in the deadlock configuration.
To satisfy the deterministic auditing system, if more than one such configuration exists, you must output the lexicographically earliest one among all valid configurations. This means you must minimize $a$; if there is a tie, minimize $b$; and if still tied, minimize $c$.

## Example 1
Input:
```
4 5
1 2
1 3
2 3
2 4
3 4
```
Output:
```
1 2 3
```

## Example 2
Input:
```
5 6
1 2
1 4
2 4
3 4
3 5
4 5
```
Output:
```
1 2 4
```
</STATEMENT>
<RATIONALE>
The description of the triangle (3-clique) was rewritten using a set-theoretic condition rather than a narrative about a "primary pair" and a "third material". This forces the model to formally interpret the requirement that any chosen material in the set of three must have the other two in its prohibition list, breaking reliance on standard textual patterns for triangles. The Input and Output sections were restored to their exact seed wording to strictly preserve all numeric bounds and formats.
</RATIONALE>
<PRESERVED_ANSWER>
The set-theoretic condition mathematically mandates that all three pairs formed by the three materials are mutually prohibited, which is identical to the original definition of a deadlock.
</PRESERVED_ANSWER>
<PRESERVED_CLASS>
The problem remains exactly equivalent to finding the lexicographically smallest 3-clique (triangle) in an undirected graph, preserving the O(n*m/w) bitset intersection complexity class.
</PRESERVED_CLASS>
<RISK>
none
</RISK>
